title: Graph Traversals: BFS, DFS & Dijkstra Made Visual
description: Master recursive DFS, iterative BFS with queues, and shortest-path Dijkstra algorithms through visual whiteboard walks and hands-on coding tests.
prerequisites: Basic Python syntax & understanding of adjacency lists

modules.title: Graph Representations (Adjacency Matrix vs List)
modules.description: Comparing spatial complexity trade-offs and when to use sparse representations.

modules.title: Breadth-First Search & Level Order Invariants
modules.description: Using double-ended queues, cycle prevention via visited sets, and shortest path in unweighted graphs.

modules.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm with Priority Queues
modules.description: Min-heap priority updates, greedy frontier exploration, and edge weight relaxations.

comments.text: The visual comparison between BFS and DFS traversal order made tree height problems so intuitive!
Question on slide 14: when edge weights are negative, why does Dijkstra fail and when should we use Bellman-Ford?

userNotes: Remember: Dijkstra fails with negative cycles because greedy assumption that closed distance is finalized gets violated. For unweighted graphs, plain BFS is O(V + E) which is faster than Dijkstra O((V + E) log V).

modules.title: Everyday Connectors & Thinking Sounds

modules.title: Campus Life Roleplay Simulation
modules.description: Ordering at a café, asking for library directions, and discussing weekend plans.

comments.text: Carlos is the best! The tongue placement tip for the trilled R made a world of difference.

userNotes: Practice phrase: "El perro de San Roque no tiene rabo". Focus on relaxed breath rather than forcing tongue tension.
